title: The wedding night
hookLine: Rumi died on 17 December 1273, and his followers call it his wedding night
carry: an ending can also be a meeting
tomorrow: three acts can be the play

cards: Every December, Konya in central Turkey fills with visitors, and night after night there's music, the reed flute, and the slow turning in white. It looks like a festival. In a way, it is.
But what it marks is a death: the anniversary of the night Rumi died, seven and a half centuries ago. His followers don't call it his funeral, or his passing. They call it his wedding.

teach.b: Şeb-i Arus is the Turkish form of a Persian phrase, shab-e arus: the wedding night.
Rumi died in Konya on the seventeenth of December, 1273, after an illness. For weeks his reed has cried for the reedbed it was cut from, and his lover has longed for the beloved.
Now think how his followers read his death through those poems. If life is separation, and the beloved is God, then death is not the end of the love story.

It's the night the lover finally meets the beloved, and the long separation is over. That's why they call it a wedding. Accounts written by his followers say Rumi asked his friends not to grieve for him.
The same accounts tell a story that people of many communities walked in his funeral procession, Muslims, Christians and Jews, each saying he had deepened their own faith.

It can't be checked, but it has long been part of how he's remembered. He was buried beside his father, and his tomb, under a green-tiled dome, is still in Konya, now a museum. Here's the honest part.
Calling a death a wedding night doesn't make grief wrong. Rumi himself wrote torrents of grief when Shams disappeared.
The tradition doesn't erase sorrow. It gives it a direction: an ending can also be a meeting. That's what the Mevlevis gather in December to remember.

how: Each December the Mevlevi community and visitors gather in Konya for Şeb-i Arus, with sema ceremonies and recitation leading up to the anniversary of Rumi's death on 17 December.

games.why: his followers call it Şeb-i Arus, the wedding night, because in his poems death is the lover's reunion with the beloved.

practice: Think of an ending in your own life: a move, a job left, a friendship that changed, a season closing; if a loss is too raw today, choose a smaller one.
Notice what you still feel, then gently ask: did this ending also bring me toward something, a person, a place, a truer version of me? Don't force an answer; let the question sit beside the sadness.
